t: Petovio and the council of war
p: The Flavianist generals argued their plan at the winter camp of the 13th legion.
b: Tacitus names Petovio, where the 13th legion spent the winter, as the place where the Flavianist leaders (the generals who had declared for Vespasian) met to decide between two plans: hold the Alpine passes and wait, or strike into Italy. The delay party points to the German legions and to Mucianus and the forces of the East still on their way. Josephus tells the same turn from the East. In his words "they declared Vespasian emperor, and exhorted him to save the government" (War 4.601), and Mucianus, "who was the president of the province," came to join him (War 4.621). Josephus does not name Petovio: the name is not anywhere in Whiston's text of the War (searched in full).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:5; Histories of Tacitus 3:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:46

t: Primus Antonius, the general who would not wait
p: A man once thrown out of the Senate becomes the driving force of the Flavianist invasion.
b: Marcus Antonius Primus was born at Tolosa (Toulouse) in Gaul and in his youth bore the nickname Becco ("a rooster's beak"), both from Suetonius (Vitellius 18). Tacitus says he had been convicted of forgery under Nero, got back his senatorial rank, and was put over the 7th legion by Galba (2:86). Wikipedia's page on him says the charge was forging a will, that he was banished, and that Galba gave him the 13th legion (Gemina) in Pannonia; Tacitus's word is the 7th. After Vitellius fell the Senate gave him the rank of a consul, and he left Rome when Mucianus came (Wikipedia). Tacitus makes him the hero of the march and later the man who spoiled his own victory (3:49). Josephus names "Antonius Primus and Mucianus" together as those who destroyed Vitellius and his German legions (War 4.495, a summary line).
r: Histories of Tacitus 2:86; Histories of Tacitus 3:3; Histories of Tacitus 3:49; Histories of Tacitus 3:52

a: Germany, where their strength comes from
t: Compared with the Bible: the frontier armies
p: The Gospels and Acts know the same army of legions, cohorts and centurions that makes emperors here.
b: Antonius lists the empire as a map of strength: Germany, Britain, Gaul, Spain, two fleets. The Bible shows the same army in small scenes. A centurion says, "I am a man under someone's authority myself, and I have soldiers under me" (Matthew 8:9). Cornelius is "a centurion in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1). Paul is turned over to "a centurion of the Emperor's Cohort, a man named Julius" (Acts 27:1). Agrees: the ranks and the chain of command are the same. Differs in weight: the New Testament has no stake in who wears the purple, while in Tacitus the armies themselves choose. This is background, not a shared event, and no person here is the same.

a: the one real general in the army
t: The soldiers make their general
p: In a civil war the army's favor counted for more than rank. Antonius won it by speaking plainly.
b: Antonius held no supreme command. The soldiers made him their general by cheering him, because at the first assembly, after Vespasian's letters were read, he had taken his side openly and so "shared with them" whatever came, "their crime or their glory." Dio, in the short version made later by Xiphilinus, also says Primus was chosen as general by the Moesian soldiers (Epitome of book 64, 9.3). Josephus too has Vespasian declared emperor: "they declared Vespasian emperor, and exhorted him to save the government" (War 4.601).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:10; Histories of Tacitus 3:49

t: Procurator
p: A procurator managed the emperor's business in a province, and some small provinces were ruled by one.
b: The Latin is procurator, the emperor's own agent. Cornelius Fuscus is one here, Portius Septimius governs Raetia as one (3:5), and Valerius Paullinus is another (3:43). Judea in the Gospels had a ruler of this rank: "Pontius Pilate was governing Judea" (Luke 3:1). After Felix, "Porcius Festus took over from Felix" (Acts 24:27). The Gospels and Acts call such men governors, so the link is the office, not a shared name.
r: Luke 3:1; Acts 24:27; Histories of Tacitus 3:5; Histories of Tacitus 3:43

t: Why Flavianus was wanted: a name of consular rank
p: A man who had been consul gave a rebel party standing in the Senate's eyes.
b: Tampius Flavianus had been consul, the highest regular office, and the Flavianist leaders wanted his name so their rising would look lawful at the start. Romans dated their years by the names of the two consuls, as Tacitus does at 3:34 ("in the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius and Publius Cornelius"). Luke dates the start of John's work another way, by a reign and by the rulers of each region: "the fifteenth year of Tiberius Caesar's rule" (Luke 3:1). Both are ways of fixing a date in the empire's own terms.
r: Luke 3:1; Luke 2:1; Histories of Tacitus 3:34; Histories of Tacitus 3:37

a: Sido and Italicus, kings of the Suevi
t: Client kings on the frontier
p: Rome let friendly kings keep their thrones on its edge. The Bible knows the same arrangement.
b: Sido and Italicus ruled the Suevi, and Tacitus says the Suevi "had long been loyal to the Romans." Kings who kept their crowns while serving Rome are the same kind of ruler as the Herods of the Bible's world. "King Agrippa came down to Caesarea with Bernice to welcome Festus" (Acts 25:13), and the Herod of Acts 12 is a king who dealt with the cities of Tyre and Sidon (Acts 12:20). Tacitus meets another such figure in Polemon of Pontus (3:47).
r: Acts 25:13; Acts 25:23; Acts 12:20; Histories of Tacitus 3:47

a: their people were faithful to any trust given them
t: A damaged word in the Latin of 3:5
p: The Latin text has a corrupt word here. The translation follows the sense of the older English.
b: Fisher's Oxford text prints gens fidei †commissior† patientior, with daggers around commissior to show an editor thought the word corrupt. The Conversational English Translation follows the sense of Church and Brodribb, "faithful to any trust given them." This is the only damaged spot marked in Book 3. See the variant entry.

t: Same name as Felix of Acts? Sextilius Felix
p: A cavalry commander named Felix holds the Aenus line. He is not the governor Felix of Acts.
b: Sextilius Felix commands a cavalry wing, eight cohorts and the levy of Noricum on the river Aenus. Acts names Felix, a governor who "left Paul behind in chains" when "Porcius Festus took over from Felix" (Acts 24:27). Same-person verdict: unlikely. The full names differ: Tacitus names the governor of Judea under Claudius Antonius Felix (5:9), and this man is Sextilius Felix, an army officer on the Danube side in AD 69.

a: Corbulo and his successes in Armenia
t: Corbulo, Armenia and Parthia
p: Arrius Varus won his name serving under Corbulo in the war over Armenia.
b: Corbulo commanded Roman armies in the East under Nero, and Armenia was the land the Romans and the Parthians fought over. The Gospels' world is that same frontier: Parthians head the list of peoples at Pentecost in Jerusalem ("We are Parthians, Medes and Elamites," Acts 2:9). In his speech to the 3rd legion Antonius lists the Parthians, the Armenians and the Sarmatae as old victories (3:24).

t: Galba's statues put back up
p: Antonius had the dead emperor's images restored to make his party look friendly to Galba's memory.
b: Galba was killed on 15 January 69: Tacitus dates the day Otho was hailed emperor to 15 January (1:27), and Book 1 has Galba killed that same day (1:41-49). His images had been pulled down in the troubles, and Antonius had them put up again in every town as a political act. Honoring or removing an emperor's image was a public sign of loyalty. The question put to Jesus about the head tax to Caesar (Matthew 22:17) belongs to the same world, where the emperor's rule was something every subject had to answer to. The imperial cult proper is on the topic page.
r: Matthew 22:17; Luke 20:25; Mark 12:17; Histories of Tacitus 1:27

a: since he held Egypt, which controls the grain supply
t: Compared with the Bible: Egypt, Alexandria and the grain
p: Vespasian planned to starve Vitellius by holding Egypt's grain. Acts shows the same grain ships.
b: Vespasian's order was to halt at Aquileia, because holding Egypt, which controls the grain, would force Vitellius's army to give in for lack of pay and food. Josephus gives the same plan: Vespasian was "intent upon gaining the dominion over Alexandria" because Egypt supplied "corn," and if he could be master of it he hoped to "dethrone Vitellius" (War 4.605-606). Agrees with Acts, which shows the trade from the Bible side: "the centurion came across a ship out of Alexandria bound for Italy" (Acts 27:6), and Paul later sails on another "ship from Alexandria" (Acts 28:11). Tacitus comes back to the plan at 3:48.

a: Mucianus said the same in frequent letters
t: Mucianus, the governor of Syria
p: Mucianus backed Vespasian but, Tacitus says, wanted the glory of finishing the war.
b: Licinius Mucianus governed neighboring Syria and promised Vespasian the Syrian army (Suetonius, Vespasian 6.4). Josephus calls him "the president of the province" (War 4.621). Syria's capital was Antioch, where "the disciples came to be called 'Christians'" (Acts 11:26). Tacitus shows Mucianus holding back the victors with ambiguous letters (3:78) and slowing Antonius (3:52). This is background for the Bible's Syria, not a link to any person in Acts.
r: Acts 11:26; Histories of Tacitus 3:46; Histories of Tacitus 3:52; Histories of Tacitus 3:78

t: Compared with the Bible: tribunes and centurions
p: The officers Caecina tries to win over are the same ranks Acts names.
b: A tribune commanded a cohort and a centurion a company. The letters read before the army offered them "the hope of keeping the privileges Vitellius had granted them." In Acts a "commander of the cohort" hears that "all Jerusalem was in chaos" and "took soldiers and centurions with him" (Acts 21:31-32). Later a commander says, "It cost me a great deal of money to acquire this citizenship" (Acts 22:28). Agrees: same ranks, and a similar link between rank and privilege: in Tacitus the privileges were granted by Vitellius, in Acts a commander paid for citizenship. No person is the same.

a: Aponius was shouted down whenever he tried to speak
t: The mutinies at Verona
p: The Flavianist army nearly killed its own commanders over a false alarm.
b: Soldiers saw allied cavalry in the distance, took them for enemies and seized their weapons. In the panic they turned on Flavianus, called him Vitellius's relative and the traitor who had betrayed Otho, and shouted down every officer but Antonius. The crowd moved from suspicion to insults, then to weapons and fists. Acts has a mob of this sort at Ephesus: "the greater part had no idea what they had gathered for" (Acts 19:32), and a city official calmed it (Acts 19:35). The likeness is only in how crowds behave.

a: stretched out his hands as a suppliant
t: Suppliant
p: Flavianus begs for his life with open hands and by lying on the ground.
b: The Latin word is supplex, one who begs for mercy. Tacitus uses the picture again when the beaten Vitellianists hold out suppliants' branches from the walls (3:31) and when Lucius Vitellius falls at the emperor's knees (3:38).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:31; Histories of Tacitus 3:38

t: Compared with the Bible: Dalmatia, Illyricum and the Adriatic
p: The fleet's sailors came from lands the New Testament also names.
b: Bassus's sailors were "natives of Dalmatia and Pannonia," provinces held for Vespasian, and the fleet was at Ravenna on the Adriatic. Paul writes, "from Jerusalem and around in a circle as far as Illyricum, I have completed the preaching of the good news of Christ" (Romans 15:19), and Titus, Paul's coworker, went to Dalmatia (2 Timothy 4:10). The sea itself is the "Adria" on which Paul's ship drifted (Acts 27:27). Agrees on the lands; the exact limits of Paul's Illyricum are not given by Tacitus, so this is a shared place-name, not a shared event.
r: Romans 15:19; 2 Timothy 4:10; Acts 27:27; Histories of Tacitus 3:35; Histories of Tacitus 3:50

a: made them swear allegiance to Vespasian
t: The soldiers' oath
p: Changing the name in the oath changed the emperor. The Gospels speak of oaths differently.
b: Caecina made the men he had called to headquarters swear to Vespasian, and the images of Vitellius were torn down, so the change of emperor was made in one meeting while most of the army was elsewhere. The soldier's oath bound him to his commander and the emperor. Jesus tells his followers, "do not take oaths at all" (Matthew 5:34), a teaching about everyday speech, not a ruling about soldiers' oaths. Whether a Christian may serve as a soldier at all is the question in the chapter's tradition card.

t: The sneer at Antonius
p: The angry soldiers call Antonius an exile, since he had been banished from Rome.
b: The soldiers say they are being handed over "as a gift to the exile Antonius." The insult only works because he had really been condemned under Nero: Tacitus says he was convicted of forgery (2:86), and Wikipedia's page on him adds that he was banished. Banishment was a common Roman penalty; John says of himself, "I was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus" (Revelation 1:9), though the book does not say who sent him.
r: Revelation 1:9; Histories of Tacitus 2:86; Histories of Tacitus 3:2

a: Soldiers get the plunder of a city taken by storm
t: Compared with the Bible: soldiers and plunder
p: The soldiers' thought is plain: a city that surrenders pays nothing. The Gospels tell soldiers the opposite.
b: In the soldiers' own private thinking, a city that surrenders pays nothing, and one taken by storm pays them. When soldiers asked John the Baptist what to do, he answered, "Don't squeeze money out of anyone by force or by false charges. Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14). Differs: the demand of the Gospel is the reverse of the army's custom here. Agrees that plunder was how soldiers expected to be paid beyond wages; Tacitus says the same of the "bonus" they cry out for at 3:50.

a: about the third hour of the night, around nine o'clock
t: The hours of the night and day
p: The Latin counts the hours of the night, not a clock. The "nine o'clock" is a modern help.
b: The Latin says tertia fere noctis hora, about the third hour of the night. Church and Brodribb turn this into "about nine o'clock at night", and the Conversational English Translation keeps "around nine o'clock" beside the Latin count as a rough help; the Latin itself gives no clock time. Wikipedia's page on Roman timekeeping says the Romans divided daylight into twelve hours and that an hour was shorter in winter and longer in summer (about 45 minutes at the winter solstice and 75 at the summer solstice), and it speaks of hours of the night too, such as "the first hour of the night". So a Roman hour is not a fixed hour on a modern clock. Acts uses the same Roman hours: a commander orders troops to march "starting at the third hour of the night" (Acts 23:23). The day was divided too: "Doesn't the day have twelve hours?" (John 11:9).

t: The legion's eagle
p: Each legion carried an eagle as its standard. Atilius Verus died saving the 7th legion's.
b: The eagle (aquila) was the legion's standard, and Atilius Verus, chief centurion of the first company, died saving it. Eagles and standards appear again when the Vitellianists give up at Cremona: "they carried out the standards and eagles" (3:31). Tacitus puts the saving of the eagle in his list of what the 7th legion suffered that night: six chief centurions killed, some standards taken, and the eagle itself saved at the cost of Verus's life.

a: saluted the rising sun, as is the custom in Syria
t: Compared with the Bible: bowing to the rising sun
p: Syrian soldiers greeted the sun. The Bible warns against that very act.
b: The 3rd legion answers Antonius with a morning salute to the sun, which Tacitus ties to the custom of Syria. Differs: Moses warned Israel, "when you raise your eyes to the sky and see the sun, the moon and the stars, the whole army of the sky, do not be pulled away to bow down to them and serve them" (Deuteronomy 4:19). Ezekiel saw about twenty-five men at the temple door who "stood with their backs to the LORD's temple, facing east, bowing low to the sun in the east" (Ezekiel 8:16). Tacitus calls it a custom and does not call it worship; the Bible's judgment on bowing to the sun is plain.

t: Mark Antony and the Parthians
p: Antonius reminds the 3rd legion of its victories under the famous Antony, not his own namesake.
b: Here "Marcus Antonius" is the triumvir, the famous Mark Antony, not Primus Antonius, though Wikipedia's page on the general says it has been suggested that he was the son of Lucius Antonius, which would make him a great-grandson of the triumvir, and gives a second possibility, descent from Gauls whom Mark Antony had made citizens. Tacitus has Antonius say the 3rd legion "had beaten the Parthians" under him, "the Armenians" under Corbulo and "recently the Sarmatae." The Parthians are the empire's old enemy (Acts 2:9).

t: "Pagani": civilians, not soldiers
p: Antonius calls the Praetorians "pagani," a word for people who are not soldiers. Church and Brodribb have "clowns."
b: The Latin word is pagani, civilians, people who are not soldiers, here used as an insult for soldiers who behave like men who have never served. The older English (Church and Brodribb) has "clowns." The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin. See the variant.

t: Compared with the Bible: brother against brother, child against parent
p: A son who kills his father unknowingly is a picture of family broken by war, as Jesus says it will be.
b: The story comes "on the authority of Vipstanus Messalla." Julius Mansuetus, a Spaniard, had a son who was drafted into the 7th legion and killed his father without knowing him. Jesus says, "One brother will hand another over to be killed, and a father will hand over his child. Children will rise up against their parents and have them executed" (Matthew 10:21; the same sentence is in Mark 13:12). The first murder in Genesis is of a brother: "Cain turned on Abel his brother and killed him" (Genesis 4:8). Differs: in Tacitus it is blind chance and the horror of civil war; in Jesus' words it is persecution. A shared picture of broken families, not a shared event.
r: Matthew 10:21; Mark 13:12; Genesis 4:8; Histories of Tacitus 3:51

a: dug a grave, and did for his father the last duty
t: Compared with the Bible: burying the father
p: The soldier's first act is to bury his father. The Gospels set this duty beside following Jesus.
b: The son lifts the body and digs a grave. To bury a father was the first duty of a son. A disciple tells Jesus, "Lord, allow me first to go off and bury my father," and Jesus answers, "Follow me. Let the dead bury their own dead" (Matthew 8:21-22). The burial topic gathers the Bible's texts. Tacitus assumes without comment that burying a father is the right thing, even in a war.

t: The tortoise (testudo)
p: Soldiers raised their shields over their heads and joined them like a turtle's shell.
b: The Latin is testudo, "tortoise." The soldiers locked their shields over their heads to storm a wall. Here Tacitus describes it twice: in the first assault (3:27) and when men climb "over a second tortoise formation" (3:28). A Roman siege also means camps around the city, and Jesus uses that picture of Jerusalem: "When you see Jerusalem being encircled by army camps, then know that her desolation has drawn near" (Luke 21:20).

t: Tacitus names his sources
p: Tacitus says which writers he follows, and admits when two of them disagree and he cannot decide.
b: Here Tacitus cannot decide whose idea it was to point the worn-out soldiers at Cremona's wealth. Messalla (Vipstanus Messalla, tribune of the 7th legion, Claudius's, 3:9) says it was Hormus's idea; Gaius Plinius blames Antonius and may be the better source, but Tacitus says "I can't easily decide." Elsewhere he gives Messalla as his authority for the father and son (3:25), and names Cluvius Rufus and Silius Italicus as the two witnesses of the talk between Sabinus and Vitellius (3:65). Luke too begins by saying he "kept careful track of all these things from the start" and wrote from "the people who saw it with their own eyes" (Luke 1:2-3). Both writers want the reader to see where the account comes from.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:25; Histories of Tacitus 3:65; Luke 1:1; Luke 1:2; Luke 1:3

a: conspicuous in his bordered robe and his lictors
t: Compared with the Bible: lictors and the rod-bearers
p: A Roman consul walked with attendants carrying rods. Acts has the same officers at Philippi.
b: Caecina came out as consul with his lictores, the attendants who walked before a magistrate, and in the bordered robe of his office. At Philippi, a Roman colony (Acts 16:12), "the magistrates sent the rod-bearers with a message: 'Set those men free'" (Acts 16:35). Agrees: the rod-bearers of Acts are attendants of the same kind, sent by the town's magistrates. The scene in Tacitus is a traitor consul parading as if his office still counted.

a: Caecina had put on a gladiator show there
t: Compared with the Bible: the arena
p: Caecina gave a gladiator show at Cremona, and gladiators fought in the war. Paul uses the arena as a picture.
b: Gladiator shows were part of city life, and Tacitus says the Cremonans' hatred of the Vitellianist side was made worse by one Caecina gave. Gladiators also fought in the war itself: Julianus was given "a city cohort and gladiators" (3:57), and gladiators held Tarracina (3:76). Paul writes, "As a mere man I fought with wild beasts at Ephesus. What is the profit for me?" (1 Corinthians 15:32), a picture drawn from the same world of arenas. Whether Paul fought in an arena or speaks in figures is a question for the 1 Corinthians pages.
r: 1 Corinthians 15:32; Histories of Tacitus 3:57; Histories of Tacitus 3:76

t: Compared with the Bible: robbing temples
p: Soldiers carried off the gifts given to the gods. Paul and the town clerk of Ephesus both mention temple robbery.
b: Tacitus says men carried off "heavy gold temple gifts," the offerings given to the gods, and were cut down by stronger men. In Acts the city clerk of Ephesus says of Paul's companions, "they are not temple robbers" (Acts 19:37), and Paul asks the person who prides himself on the law, "You detest idols. Do you rob temples?" (Romans 2:22). Agrees: the New Testament treats temple robbery as a recognized offense. The last sentence of 3:33 tells how one temple, of Mefitis, outside the walls, was left standing.

a: only the temple of Mefitis outside the walls remained standing
t: The temple of Mefitis
p: One shrine outside the walls survived. Tacitus offers two reasons and does not choose.
b: Tacitus says the temple of Mefitis was spared "protected by where it stood or by the power of the god," and he lets both reasons stand. He names the god Mefitis and says nothing more about her. How the Bible speaks of the gods of the nations, and how Christian readers have understood them, is on the idolatry topic page; Tacitus himself leaves the question of the god's power open.

a: in the 286th year since its founding
t: The end of Cremona
p: A colony founded in the time of Hannibal is wrecked in the Flavianist war.
b: Tacitus counts 286 years from Cremona's founding "in the consulship of Tiberius Sempronius and Publius Cornelius." He adds that it was founded when Hannibal was threatening Italy, as a bulwark against the Gauls beyond the Padus. The battle was on 24 October 69 (Wikipedia on the Second Battle of Bedriacum), and Antonius afterward banned keeping Cremonans as captives; many were then killed by their captors. Tacitus says relatives bought some back and the town was rebuilt, and Vespasian encouraged it. Roman colonies appear in the Bible, too: "Philippi, one of the foremost cities of its district of Macedonia, and a colony" (Acts 16:12).
r: Acts 16:12; Histories of Tacitus 3:32; Histories of Tacitus 3:33

a: Publilius Sabinus, prefect of the Praetorian Guard
t: Compared with the Bible: the Praetorian Guard and the praetorium
p: The emperor's guard in Rome is the likeliest meaning of the "praetorium" in Philippians.
b: The Praetorian Guard was the guard kept at Rome, with its cohorts and its prefects (here Vitellius puts one in chains and names another, Alfenus Varus; see also 3:55 and 3:58). Paul writes, "My chains are now seen for what they are, chains for Christ, by the whole praetorium and by everyone else" (Philippians 1:13). The site's Philippians page lays out the views: the guard in Rome, or a governor's headquarters (Rome, Ephesus and Caesarea have each been proposed). The site's note on Acts 28 says that over two years many guards would have heard Paul. Agrees on the institution; no person here appears in Philippians.
r: Philippians 1:13; Philippians 4:22; Acts 28:16; Histories of Tacitus 3:55

t: Compared with the Bible: authorities, flatterers and a bad emperor
p: The Senate flatters a man it despises. Paul tells Christians to submit and to pray for rulers like him.
b: Tacitus shows senators praising Vitellius while saying nothing against the Flavianists, and a man who "flattered his way" into a one-day consulship. Paul wrote to Christians in Rome, "Every person must submit to the authorities above them. There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and "If it is the tax, pay the tax" (Romans 13:7). Peter says, "Submit to the king as the one ranked highest" (1 Peter 2:13). Timothy is told to pray "for kings and for all who hold high office" (1 Timothy 2:2). Answers: these words were written to Christians who lived under emperors, and they say nothing there about exceptions. Peter and the apostles also say, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29). Churches weigh the two differently; the topic page on church and state sets out how.
r: Romans 13:1; Romans 13:7; 1 Peter 2:13; 1 Timothy 2:2; Titus 3:1; Acts 5:29

t: Compared with the Bible: a rival who is called a king
p: Lucius Vitellius frightens the emperor with a rival of royal blood. In John, Pilate is frightened the same way.
b: Lucius says Blaesus "boasts of Junii and Antonii among his ancestors, and, claiming imperial blood, he shows off his friendliness and splendor to the soldiers." The charge is that a man might be a rival to the emperor. In John 19 the crowd shouts at Pilate, "Free this man and you are no Friend of Caesar! Anyone who makes himself a king is speaking against Caesar" (John 19:12). Luke 23:2 has the charge "he says that he himself is Messiah, a king." Agrees: the same weapon, a charge of kingship, which an emperor feared. Differs: Blaesus had done nothing, and Jesus said, "My kingdom does not come from this world" (John 18:36).
r: John 19:12; Luke 23:2; John 18:36; Histories of Tacitus 3:39

a: fed his eyes on the sight of his enemy's death
t: Compared with the Bible: gloating over an enemy
p: Vitellius boasts that he fed his eyes on the dying Blaesus. Proverbs says not to.
b: Tacitus says he will give Vitellius's savage remark in his exact words, and the remark is that he "fed his eyes" on the sight. Proverbs says, "When your enemy falls, do not be glad, and when he trips, keep your heart from cheering" (Proverbs 24:17). Differs: Vitellius takes the pleasure the Bible forbids.

a: who had commanded the 2nd legion there under Claudius
t: Compared with the Bible: Claudius, Vespasian in Britain and the famine
p: Vespasian served in Britain under Claudius, the emperor of the famine and the order against the Jews in Rome.
b: Suetonius says Vespasian was sent to Germany under Claudius and then to Britain, where he "fought thirty battles with the enemy" (Vespasian 4.1). Claudius is the emperor named in Acts: "A great famine was going to strike the whole inhabited world. It did come, in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28), and "Claudius had given orders that all the Jews must leave Rome" (Acts 18:2). Same person: certain, the same Claudius. Vespasian is not named in the New Testament. Suetonius says he was sent to put down the revolt in Judea (Vespasian 4.5), the war that most readers connect with Jesus' words on Jerusalem in Luke 21:20-24.

t: Compared with the Bible: Spain
p: The 1st legion in Spain goes over to Vespasian. Paul planned to travel to Spain.
b: Tacitus names the 1st legion, the Adjutrix, in Spain as the first to go over after Valens was taken. In Romans Paul says, "when I make my trip to Spain. I hope to see you on my way through" (Romans 15:24). Agrees that Spain was a Roman province with legions in AD 69. Whether Paul ever went is not in Acts or in Tacitus.

t: Compared with the Bible: the rumor that rulers would come from Judea
p: Suetonius says an old belief held that men from Judea would rule the world, and applies it to Vespasian.
b: Suetonius writes that there was an old belief that "it was fated at that time for men coming from Judaea to rule the world," that the Judeans applied it to themselves, and that it really pointed to Vespasian (Vespasian 4.5). Tacitus tells it in Book 5 (5:13): "Most were convinced that the ancient writings of their priests said that at this very time the East would grow strong and men setting out from Judea would rule the world," and "Those riddles had really predicted Vespasian and Titus." Compared with the Bible: the Jewish hope of a coming king is the Bible's own (see the topic on the Messiah).

t: Cartismandua, Caratacus and the triumph of Claudius
p: Tacitus says Cartismandua gave Rome the British king Caratacus and so adorned Claudius's triumph.
b: Cartismandua, queen of the Brigantes in northern Britain, handed Caratacus over to Rome "by trickery," and this made her seem to have "adorned the triumph of Claudius Caesar." Then she left her husband Venutius for his armor-bearer Vellocatus, and the people took the husband's side. The Roman troops saved her but left the kingdom to Venutius. Claudius is the Claudius of Acts 11:28 and Acts 18:2.

t: Compared with the Bible: royal wives and new husbands
p: A queen leaves her husband for another man. The Herods' family and Felix's wife Drusilla did the same.
b: Herodias had been "the wife of his brother Philip" when Herod "had married her" (Mark 6:17), and John the Baptist told Herod, "The law does not allow you to have your brother's wife" (Mark 6:18). Josephus says that Drusilla's marriage to Azizus, king of Emesa, ended "in no long time," and she "was prevailed upon to transgress the laws of her forefathers, and to marry Felix" (Antiquities 20.141-143); Acts says "Felix came with Drusilla, his own wife, a Jewish woman" (Acts 24:24). One caution on Drusilla: Tacitus says Felix's wife Drusilla was a granddaughter of Antony and Cleopatra (5:9), while Josephus and Acts have the Jewish Drusilla, Agrippa's sister, so the writers do not describe the same woman. Same-person verdict: none of these is Cartismandua; the link is the pattern of royal marriages arranged or broken under Roman power.
r: Mark 6:17; Mark 6:18; Acts 24:24; Histories of Tacitus 5:9

a: Fonteius Agrippa was moved from Asia, which he had governed for a year as proconsul
t: Compared with the Bible: proconsuls and Asia
p: A proconsul governed Asia for one year. Acts speaks of proconsuls in Ephesus, Cyprus and Achaia.
b: Tacitus calls Fonteius Agrippa a proconsul of Asia, a governor who held the post for a year. Acts says, "there are proconsuls" at Ephesus (Acts 19:38), names "the proconsul Sergius Paulus" (Acts 13:7), and "Gallio ... serving as proconsul of Achaia" (Acts 18:12). Same-person verdict: Fonteius Agrippa is not King Agrippa of Acts 25 (unlikely): he is a Roman senator, the king a Jewish ruler. The name Agrippa is shared; the men are not.

t: Compared with the Bible: Polemon, Pontus and the Jewish princess Berenice
p: Anicetus was freedman of a king whose Pontic kingdom became a province. That king married a Jewish queen.
b: Tacitus says Anicetus was a freedman of Polemon and that Pontus had been turned into a province (3:47). Suetonius says Nero added Pontus to the provinces "when it was given up by Polemon" (Nero 18), with no year. Josephus says that Berenice, a daughter of Agrippa, "persuaded Poleme, who was king of Cilicia, to be circumcised, and to marry her," that Berenice then left him, and that he gave up the marriage and "the Jewish religion" (Antiquities 20.145-146). A Wikipedia page on Polemon II says he ruled Pontus and Cilicia and married Berenice. Same-person verdict, Tacitus's Polemon and Berenice's husband: likely: both are a Polemon who ruled Pontus and, in Josephus, Cilicia, and Suetonius ties the loss of Pontus to Polemon. Acts names a Bernice at King Agrippa's side before Festus (Acts 25:13, 25:23), the well-known sister of Agrippa II.

t: Compared with the Bible: Pontus and the Black Sea
p: Pontus is the land of Aquila and the first readers of 1 Peter.
b: The tribes of the Pontic coast, and Trapezus on the "far edge of the Pontic coast," belong to the same region the New Testament names. Pontus is in the list of peoples at Pentecost (Acts 2:9), it is where Aquila came from ("a man of Pontus by birth," Acts 18:2), and Peter writes to the Dispersion "in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia and Bithynia" (1 Peter 1:1). Agrees on the region.

t: Camarae, the barbarian boats
p: The raiders' boats had planks added as the sea rose, until they were closed like a house.
b: The Latin name is camarae, a word Tacitus says they used. He describes narrow sides, a broad belly, no bronze or iron in the joins, and planks built up as the waves rise until the boat is "closed in like a house." With a prow at each end and oars that can be switched, the boat lands either way.

t: Compared with the Bible: Alexandria
p: Vespasian hurried to the Egyptian city that gave Acts its Alexandrian ship and its Apollos.
b: Tacitus has Vespasian go to Alexandria, in Egypt, the land whose grain fed Rome. Acts names "a Jew called Apollos, an Alexandrian by birth" (Acts 18:24), "the Alexandrians" in the argument with Stephen (Acts 6:9), and the grain ship "from Alexandria" (Acts 27:6; Acts 28:11). Suetonius says the first legions to swear to Vespasian were in Egypt under its prefect Tiberius Alexander (Vespasian 6.3). Agrees on the city; the Bible has no link to Vespasian's stay.

t: Compared with the Bible: famine as a weapon
p: Vespasian planned to squeeze the city with hunger. The Bible knows famine as a plague and a sign.
b: Vespasian meant to cut off the grain and make Vitellius's side hungry (3:8, 3:48). The Bible speaks of famine in the Roman age too: "a great famine was going to strike the whole inhabited world. It did come, in the days of Claudius" (Acts 11:28). Jesus lists it among the signs: "There will be great earthquakes, and famines and plagues in place after place" (Luke 21:11). Differs: in Tacitus famine is a general's tool; in the Gospels it is part of the world's trouble that Jesus told his disciples not to panic over (Matthew 24:6-7). The topic on famine gathers the Bible's cases.

t: Clavarium: the soldiers' bonus
p: The soldiers shout for a Latin word that means a bonus. The translation gives the meaning.
b: The Latin word is clavarium, which Tacitus says "is the word for the bonus." It was an extra payment demanded by the soldiers during the march, when neither money nor grain had been provided. The Conversational English Translation keeps the Latin name in the text so a reader sees what the soldiers actually shouted. The Gospels' only advice to soldiers is "Make do with your pay" (Luke 3:14).

t: Earlier civil wars: Cinna, Pompey and Sisenna
p: Tacitus compares the cavalryman's boast with an older story from the civil wars of the Republic.
b: The old story is of a soldier on Pompey's side who killed his brother in the battle at the Janiculum against Cinna and, learning it, killed himself, "as Sisenna tells it." Tacitus uses it to say that earlier generations felt such crimes more sharply. The Gospels have only the saying about brother handing over brother (Matthew 10:21), noted at 3:25.

t: Compared with the Bible: truth at the cost of life
p: Agrestis ends his life to prove he told the truth. The Bible tells of others who ended theirs, without praise.
b: The centurion's last words were meant to prove that he had not been bribed. The site's topic on suicide gathers the Bible's few cases: Saul (1 Samuel 31:4), Ahithophel (2 Samuel 17:23) and Judas, who "regretted it," "flung the silver into the sanctuary" and "hanged himself" (Matthew 27:3-5). Differs: in each Bible case the death follows a failure of plan or betrayal; in Tacitus it is the soldier's last proof of honesty. Tacitus praises his steadfastness (Church and Brodribb: "Singular bravery") and does not comment on the act itself.

t: Same name as Julius of Acts? Julius Agrestis
p: A centurion named Julius goes to see the enemy for Vitellius. Acts has a centurion named Julius.
b: Acts says Paul and other prisoners were turned over "to a centurion of the Emperor's Cohort, a man named Julius" (Acts 27:1). Agrestis is a Vitellianist centurion in AD 69 who goes to Antonius's camp and back. Same-person verdict: unlikely. Acts gives only the name Julius, and Julius is also the name of other men in this book (Julius Mansuetus 3:25, Julius Flavianus 3:79, Julius Placidus 3:84). Nothing in Acts or in Tacitus ties Agrestis, a Vitellianist centurion who goes to Antonius's camp and back, to Paul's escort.

t: Compared with the Bible: citizenship given and bought, and tribute
p: Vitellius gave out citizenship and tax relief to win friends. In Acts a commander says he paid for his.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius "handed out treaties to allies and Latin rights to foreigners" and "relieved some of tribute and others of duties." Roman citizenship and rights were a gift an emperor could sell or give. In Acts a commander says, "It cost me a great deal of money to acquire this citizenship," and Paul answers, "I, though, was born to it" (Acts 22:28). Paul also tells the Romans, "If it is the tax, pay the tax. If it is the customs duty, pay the duty" (Romans 13:7). Agrees that rights and taxes could be given or sold; Tacitus says the wise thought such gifts worthless because they ruined the state.

a: he tore the empire to pieces
t: Lacerare imperium
p: The Latin says Vitellius "mangled" the empire; the older English says he "mutilated its resources."
b: The Latin verb is lacerare, to tear or mangle. Church and Brodribb have "mutilated the resources of the Empire," which narrows it to money. The Conversational English Translation follows the Latin, since the list before it (treaties, citizenship, tax relief) is about giving away the empire itself, not only its income. See the variant.

t: Compared with the Bible: omens and sacrifice
p: A cloud of birds and a runaway bull were read as signs from the gods. The Law forbids looking for omens.
b: The Romans read birds, sacrifices and strange events as messages from the gods. A bull that broke from the altar and was struck down "not in the way victims are struck" was a bad sign, and so were the birds that hid the day. The Law of Moses said, "There must not be found among you ... anyone who practices divination, reads signs, looks for omens or works sorcery" (Deuteronomy 18:10). In Acts the priest of Zeus at Lystra "brought bulls and wreaths of flowers to the gates" (Acts 14:13). Differs: Rome sought a message in the animal; the Bible tells God's people to listen to God instead. Jesus also speaks of "great signs from the sky" before the end (Luke 21:11).

a: Puteoli was especially keen for Vespasian
t: Compared with the Bible: Puteoli
p: Puteoli, where Paul landed in Italy, takes Vespasian's side.
b: Tacitus says the Misenum fleet and towns of Campania turned to Vespasian, "Puteoli was especially keen" while Capua stayed loyal to Vitellius. Puteoli is where Paul first landed on his way to Rome: "by the second day we were at Puteoli. There we met some brothers, who urged us to remain with them for seven days" (Acts 28:13-14). Agrees on the place. Since Paul found believers at Puteoli (Acts 28:14), Christians were there before Tacitus's year; the New Testament says no more.

t: Compared with the Bible: Caesar as a title
p: Vitellius, who had refused the name Caesar, now asks for it. The New Testament uses it as the emperor's title.
b: The name Caesar began as a family name of Julius Caesar and had become the title of an emperor. Tacitus says Vitellius "refused before" and now asked for it, out of superstition about the name. The New Testament uses it only as the ruling title: "an order came out from Caesar Augustus" (Luke 2:1), "Pay back to Caesar what belongs to Caesar" (Mark 12:17), and Paul's "I appeal to Caesar!" (Acts 25:11). Domitian is "hailed as Caesar" in the last verse of this book (3:86).
r: Luke 2:1; Mark 12:17; Acts 25:11; Histories of Tacitus 3:86

t: Compared with the Bible: freedmen
p: Former slaves who had become free offered to serve Vitellius. The Bible names a synagogue of the Freedmen.
b: Freedmen are former slaves, and under the empire many of them held real power, running the emperor's offices. Acts 6:9 speaks of "the synagogue called the Freedmen's." The site's Philippians note on Caesar's household (Philippians 4:22) says the emperor's household included many slaves and former slaves who ran his palace and his offices. Agrees on the class; the people are not named in common.

t: Domitian in 69
p: Vespasian's younger son was in Rome in December 69, under guard, and he was hailed as Caesar at the end.
b: Domitian is Vespasian's son, brother of Titus (Suetonius, Vespasian 3.1). In Tacitus he was in Rome in the guard of Vitellius, who out of family feeling did him no harm. Messengers from Antonius offered to rescue him, and he had the courage but the guards were not trusted (3:59). He escapes from the Capitol in disguise at 3:74. The site's Revelation page dates that book probably to about AD 95, under Domitian, and notes that some date it to the late 60s.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:74; Histories of Tacitus 3:86; Revelation 1:9

a: At the Juvenalia games under Nero he acted in farces
t: Valens and Nero's Juvenalia
p: Fabius Valens, killed in December 69, had acted on stage in Nero's time.
b: Tacitus says Valens took part in the Juvenalia games under Nero and acted in farces, "at first as if forced and later by choice." He also says Valens first backed Verginius and then slandered him, and that he murdered Fonteius Capito. The site's topic on Nero has the emperor's reign (54 to 68) and the fire of Rome in 64. Valens is a Vitellianist commander; his head, shown to the Vitellianist cohorts, ended their hope (3:62).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:40; Histories of Tacitus 3:41

a: Caesar did not leave Pompey alive, and Augustus did not leave Antony
t: Compared with the Bible: Pompey, Augustus and Claudius
p: Vitellius's friends name three rulers Rome and the Bible also name: Pompey, Augustus and Claudius.
b: They tell Vitellius that no winner leaves a rival alive: "Caesar did not leave Pompey alive, and Augustus did not leave Antony." Augustus is the emperor of Luke 2:1 ("an order came out from Caesar Augustus"): same person, certain. Claudius, named in the speech (Vitellius's father was "Claudius's colleague"), is the Claudius of Acts 11:28 and 18:2, certain. Pompey is the general who, in Tacitus's words at 5:9, was the first Roman to conquer the Jews and entered their Temple (the site's topic on Rome); the Bible does not name him. Tacitus says Pompey was the first Roman to conquer the Jews (5:9).
r: Luke 2:1; Acts 11:28; Acts 18:2; Histories of Tacitus 5:9

t: The dates of the last days
p: Tacitus dates Vitellius's surrender to 18 December. Other writers date his death to 20 December.
b: Tacitus gives 18 December as the day Vitellius, hearing that the legion and cohorts at Narnia had gone over, left the Palace in mourning dress and offered to give up the throne in an assembly. Wikipedia's page on the year of the four emperors gives 20 December 69 for Vitellius's death, and 21 December for the Senate's recognition of Vespasian. Dio's account, in the Epitome that survives, gives no calendar date for the death (Epitome of book 64, 22). Tacitus gives the date of Rosius Regulus's one day as consul as 31 October (3:37).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:37; Histories of Tacitus 3:85

a: unfastened the dagger from his side
t: Compared with the Bible: the sword and the power over life and death
p: Vitellius offers the consul his dagger, giving back the power over life and death.
b: Vitellius took the dagger from his side and held it out "as a sign of giving back the power of death and life over citizens." That power belonged to rulers. Paul says of the ruler, "It does not carry the sword for no reason. It is God's servant, an avenger to carry out anger on the person who does evil" (Romans 13:4). Pilate tells Jesus, "you know I have the power to set you free, and the power to crucify you?" and Jesus answers, "You would not have any power against me, none, if it had not been granted to you from above" (John 19:10-11). Agrees that Rome treated the power over life as a gift tied to office; answers it by placing that gift under God.

t: The short reigns of 69 and Revelation 17:10
p: Tacitus lists how earlier emperors fell. The Revelation page counts these reigns for the seven kings.
b: Tacitus lists the ends of Caesar, Gaius, Nero, Piso and Galba, and he is watching the end of Vitellius. Revelation says of the seven kings, "Five have fallen. One is. The other has not yet come, and when he comes he must stay for a short time" (Revelation 17:10). The site's Revelation page lists the ways readers count: from Julius Caesar, giving Nero as "one is"; from Augustus, giving Galba; or from Augustus while skipping the three short reigns of 68-69, giving Vespasian. Other readers take the seven as seven world empires, or as a symbol of completeness, and then the emperors do not matter. Which count is right changes the date of Revelation. Tacitus does not mention Revelation; this note only shows the dates he narrates. Tacitus dates the day Galba fell to 15 January 69 (1:27), and Wikipedia's page on the year gives Otho's death as 16 April and Vitellius's as 20 December.

a: The rumor that he was giving up the throne had gotten there first
t: Where verse 68 ends
p: The Latin starts verse 69 at this sentence. The site follows the older English, which ends verse 68 with it.
b: In Fisher's Latin the sentence Praevenerat rumor ("The rumor had run ahead") opens section 69. Church and Brodribb's English puts it at the end of section 68, and the site's verse boundaries follow the English. A reader comparing the Latin will find the sentence one verse later. Sabinus's written orders to the tribunes in this sentence are the first move of the story that takes him to the Capitol (3:69).

a: occupied the citadel of the Capitol
t: Sabinus takes the Capitol
p: The prefect of the city fled to the citadel with a mixed group of soldiers, senators and women.
b: The Capitol had a citadel (arx) on its hill that could be held like a fort. Tacitus names Flavius Sabinus, Vespasian's brother, as the man who took it; Josephus too says Sabinus, hearing that Antonius was near, "in the night time seized upon the capitol" (War 4.645). Tacitus adds that women went with them, above all Verulana Gratilla, "who followed no children or relatives, only the war," and that Sabinus brought in his own children and his nephew Domitian that night. Dio says Sabinus and Atticus were arrested and sent to Vitellius (Epitome of book 64, 17.3).
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:73; Histories of Tacitus 3:75

t: Same name as Cornelius of Acts? Cornelius Martialis
p: Sabinus sends a chief centurion named Cornelius. Acts has a centurion named Cornelius in Caesarea.
b: Acts says, "A man named Cornelius lived in Caesarea. He was a centurion in the unit called the Italian Cohort" (Acts 10:1). Martialis carries Sabinus's message to Vitellius and is later cut down on the Capitol (3:73). Same-person verdict: unlikely. Cornelius is also the name of other men in this book (Cornelius Fuscus 3:4, Cornelius Primus 3:74), the Cornelius of Acts is at Caesarea in Judea and Martialis is in Rome in 69, and nothing in Acts 10 or Tacitus 3:70 and 3:73 links them.

a: So the Capitol burned to the ground with its gates shut
t: Compared with the Bible: a temple burned
p: The burning of Rome's greatest temple is told in the same plain way the Bible tells the burning of Solomon's.
b: Tacitus: the Capitol "burned to the ground with its gates shut, and no one defended it and no one plundered it." The Bible has the same event for Jerusalem in 586 BC: "He set the LORD's house on fire, and the king's house, and all the houses of Jerusalem" (2 Kings 25:9), and "They set God's house on fire and tore down Jerusalem's wall" (2 Chronicles 36:19). Differs: the Babylonians burned a foreign enemy's temple; here Romans burned their own. Jesus foretold that the buildings of the temple of his day would be knocked down: "Here not one stone will be left on a stone. Every one will be knocked down" (Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6). Josephus tells that the temple burned in AD 70, on the tenth day of the month Lous, the day it had been burned by the king of Babylon (War 6.4.5, Whiston's numbering). The Jerusalem temple fell the year after this fire (the site's topic on the Temple).
r: 2 Kings 25:9; 2 Chronicles 36:19; Mark 13:2; Luke 21:6; Histories of Tacitus 4:54

a: Here there's doubt whether the attackers threw fire onto the roofs
t: Who set the Capitol on fire? Five ancient accounts
p: Tacitus says no one knows. Josephus and Dio name Vitellius's soldiers, Suetonius names Vitellius himself, and Plutarch names no cause.
b: Tacitus says it is doubtful whether the attackers or the besieged started the fire, and that the second story is "the more common." He adds that no one plundered the Capitol. Josephus says "the soldiers also plundered the temple of its ornaments, and set it on fire" (War 4.649), and the soldiers he means came from Germany. Dio (in the later Epitome) says Vitellius's soldiers, "after plundering all the votive offerings burned down the great temple and other buildings" (17.3). Suetonius makes Vitellius himself the one who set it alight: "Then he set fire to the temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and destroyed them, viewing the battle and the fire from the house of Tiberius, where he was feasting" (Vitellius 15); "them" are Sabinus and the Flavians. Plutarch says the temple "was destroyed, during the troublous times of Vitellius" and names no cause (Publicola 15). So Tacitus is the only one who leaves open that the defenders may have caused it, and the only one who says it went unplundered. Quintus Atticus later claims the crime himself (3:75).

a: the seat of Jupiter Best and Greatest
t: Jupiter Best and Greatest and his temple
p: The Capitol held Rome's chief temple, with Jupiter in the middle between Juno and Minerva.
b: The Latin of this verse is Iovis Optimi Maximi, "of Jupiter Best and Greatest" (the genitive; the dictionary form is Iuppiter Optimus Maximus). Wikipedia's page on the temple says Jupiter stood in the middle room (cella), Juno Regina on the left and Minerva on the right; Livy dated its dedication to 509 BC, and Dionysius of Halicarnassus to 507 BC. Wikipedia adds that the robe on the god's statue became the standard dress of a general celebrating a triumph. The Sibylline Books were kept there, and burned in the first fire of 83 BC. Tacitus tells the story of the temple in this verse: vowed by Tarquinius Priscus, built up by Servius Tullius and Tarquinius Superbus, and dedicated by Horatius Pulvillus.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:71; Histories of Tacitus 3:74

t: Compared with the Bible: two temples, two holy hills, one tax
p: For Rome the Capitol was a pledge of empire; for Israel the temple on Mount Moriah was the LORD's house.
b: Tacitus calls the Capitol a "pledge of empire," the sign that Rome's rule would last. The Bible's temple stood on another hill: "Solomon began building the LORD's house in Jerusalem. It stood on Mount Moriah" (2 Chronicles 3:1). After the war Vespasian laid a tribute on the Jews "wheresoever they were" and "enjoined every one of them to bring two drachmae every year into the Capitol, as they used to pay the same to the temple at Jerusalem" (Josephus, War 7.218). Answers: the Jewish temple tax was turned into a payment to Rome's temple. The rebuilding of the Capitol, which Vespasian began, is told on the topic page.

a: destroyed by the madness of emperors
t: Claude's theory: a pair of fires
p: Rome grieves its own burned temple in December 69; the next year the Romans destroy the temple in Jerusalem.
b: Claude's theory, labeled as such; the chapter page sets it out. Tacitus calls the burning of the Capitol "the saddest and most shameful" thing to happen to Rome since its founding. The next year Titus took Jerusalem, and its temple burned (Josephus, War 6.4.5), the temple of which Jesus had said, "Here not one stone will be left on a stone" (Mark 13:2). The two fires were not set by the same army: Josephus has the soldiers who came from Germany for Vitellius burn the Capitol (War 4.649), while Titus was sent to Jerusalem by Vespasian with "a select part of his army" from the East (War 4.658), and Vespasian's side won the war in which the Capitol burned. Tacitus himself shows a different ancient reading of the Capitol fire: the Gauls took it as a sign that Roman rule was ending (4:54).

a: That was the temple that was then burning.
t: The Capitol after the fire
p: Vespasian rebuilt it and it burned again in AD 80. Domitian built the fourth temple.
b: Wikipedia's page on the temple gives the later history: Sulla's rebuilding was finished in 69 BC (Tacitus names Lutatius Catulus as the name that stayed on it); the fire of AD 69 destroyed the second temple; Vespasian rebuilt it and it was dedicated in AD 75; the third temple burned in AD 80; and Domitian's fourth was finished in AD 82. Plutarch says the Capitol was burned again "upon the death of Vespasian" (Publicola 15), and Dio tells of a fire in Titus's reign that consumed "the temple of Jupiter Capitolinus" (66.24). Suetonius says Vespasian "was the first to lend a hand in clearing away the debris" (Vespasian 8.5). Wikipedia says Domitian's temple is thought to have lasted more or less intact for over three hundred years; it was the one in place when Tacitus wrote.

a: a linen robe, mixed in with a crowd of worshippers
t: Domitian's escape
p: Domitian escaped the burning Capitol in disguise. The ancient writers agree he got away; the details differ.
b: Tacitus: Domitian hid with the temple-keeper, then put on a linen robe and mixed in with worshippers, and hid at the house of Cornelius Primus. Suetonius says he escaped "in the garb of a follower of Isis" (Domitian 1). Josephus says he "providentially escaped" with other leading Romans (War 4.649), and Dio that he and the younger Sabinus escaped "in the first confusion" (Epitome of book 64, 17.4). The ancient writers agree that he escaped.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:59; Histories of Tacitus 3:86

a: a huge temple to Jupiter the Guardian, with himself in the god's lap
t: Claude's reading of an old idea: Domitian, "our Lord and God"
p: Domitian put himself in the god's lap. Suetonius says a letter in his name began "Our Master and our God."
b: Claude's reading of an idea that is not new. Suetonius says Domitian built a temple to Jupiter the Guardian on the Capitoline hill (Domitian 5) and that a circular letter issued in the name of his procurators began, "Our Master and our God bids that this be done," after which people addressed him that way (Domitian 13). Revelation 4:11 praises, "You are worthy, our Lord and God" (Revelation 4:11), and Thomas says to Jesus, "My Lord and my God!" (John 20:28). A common argument for dating Revelation under Domitian, about AD 95 (the date the site's Revelation page gives), is that the cry in Revelation 4:11 answers the emperor's title. Floyd O. Parker, in Biblica 82 (2001), pages 207-231, argues against it: he finds "Lord and God" as a divine title in the Septuagint and other Jewish sources and concludes that it cannot help date Revelation (only the article's abstract page was read). Wikipedia's article on Domitian says that Brian Jones argues the phrases came from flatterers, since Domitian issued no official documents or coins that use them. So the title alone does not date the book; it fits the Domitian date only if that date is argued on other grounds.

a: He had served the state for thirty-five years
t: Flavius Sabinus, the elder brother
p: Tacitus sums up the life of Vespasian's brother: 35 years of service, 7 in Moesia, 12 as prefect of the city.
b: Tacitus says Sabinus served 35 years, governed Moesia for seven and was prefect of the city for twelve; his only fault was talking too much. He is Vespasian's brother. Wikipedia's page on a different man, Titus Flavius Sabinus, consul in AD 69, says Townend identifies that consul as Vespasian's nephew, so the two should not be mixed up. Mucianus was pleased at his death, Tacitus has heard, and many said peace was served by ending the rivalry between Mucianus and Sabinus, one of whom thought of himself as the emperor's partner in power and the other as the emperor's brother. Quintius Atticus, the consul taken with him, offered himself as the one who burned the Capitol.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:65; Histories of Tacitus 3:71

t: Compared with the Bible: wronged envoys
p: The Senate's envoys were beaten by soldiers. David's envoys were shamed by Hanun, and war followed.
b: Tacitus: the praetor Arulenus Rusticus was wounded and his lictor killed, and "the sacred right of envoys, respected even among foreign peoples," would have been broken by Roman citizens. In the Bible, King Hanun of the Ammonites "shaved half the beard off each man" of David's envoys and cut their robes (2 Samuel 10:4), "David heard about it and sent men to meet them, since they were badly shamed" (2 Samuel 10:5), and the Ammonites knew they had made themselves hated and hired soldiers for the war (2 Samuel 10:6). Agrees that harming envoys was a grave offense in both worlds.

t: Compared with the Bible: Stoic teachers and soldiers
p: A Stoic teacher lectured armed men on peace. Paul met Stoics in Athens, but there is no direct link.
b: Musonius Rufus was a Stoic philosopher, banished by Nero (Wikipedia). Soldiers found him funny and tiresome, and some wanted to trample him. Acts says "Some of the Epicurean and Stoic philosophers also took him on" (Acts 17:18), and Paul tells them, "Even some of the poets of your own people have said it" (Acts 17:28). Same-person verdict: Musonius is not a person named in Acts, and the Wikipedia page on him names no New Testament link. The match is the type: a street teacher arguing with the crowds and soldiers.

a: he was dragged out by Julius Placidus
t: How the four ancient accounts tell Vitellius's death
p: The writers agree he was found, led through the city and killed. They differ on details.
b: Tacitus: found hiding, bound and led along while the crowd jeered, then killed at the Gemoniae. Josephus: Vitellius came out "in his cups" and "had his head cut off in the midst of Rome" (War 4.651-652). Dio (Epitome of book 64): dragged through the city and mocked, struck down at the Stairway, his head carried through the city (20.2-21.2). Suetonius: dragged to the Forum with a noose and killed at the Stairs of Wailing (Vitellius 17). The writers agree on the main events. Tacitus is the only one of the four who names Julius Placidus: the name is not in Suetonius's Vitellius, in Dio's Epitome of books 64 and 65, or in Josephus's account of the death of Vitellius (War 4.11.4, Whiston's numbering), checked in the texts.

t: The Gemonian Stairs
p: The Gemonian Stairs were the steps where Rome's hated dead were left. Suetonius calls them the Stairs of Wailing.
b: Sabinus's body had lain there (3:74), and now Vitellius's was brought. Suetonius puts his death at the Stairs of Wailing and says the body was dragged to the Tiber; Thayer's note on the page says the "wailing" explanation of the name is probably false, although it was current in antiquity (Vitellius 17). Tacitus reports one saying of his at the end, to a tribune who insulted him: "Yet I was your emperor," and then he fell.
r: Histories of Tacitus 3:74; Histories of Tacitus 3:84

t: Vitellius's age
p: Tacitus and Suetonius count his 57th year, but Suetonius's own birth date makes him 54, as Dio's epitome says.
b: Tacitus says Vitellius was "completing his 57th year." Suetonius says he died "in the fifty-seventh year of his age" (Vitellius 18). Suetonius also gives his birth as the eighth day before the Kalends of October (or, some say, the seventh before the Ides of September) in the consulship of Drusus Caesar and Norbanus Flaccus (Vitellius 3); Wikipedia's page on Vitellius dates his birth to 24 September AD 15. Counted from that date he was 54 in December 69, which is what the Epitome of Dio gives: "fifty-four years and eighty-nine days," and a reign of "a year lacking ten days" (Epitome of book 64, 22). The 57th-year count in the two Latin writers does not fit Suetonius's own birth date. Church and Brodribb have "nearly completed" for the Latin explebat; the Conversational English Translation has "was completing." See the variant.

t: Domitian hailed as Caesar
p: The Flavianist side made Domitian "Caesar" at once, as their pledge of Vespasian's house.
b: With no enemy left to fear, Domitian came forward to the party leaders and was hailed as Caesar, and the soldiers took him to his father's house. Tacitus says Vespasian's reign began at Alexandria, where Tiberius Alexander made the legions swear to him on 1 July, and that the army of Judea swore on 3 July (2:79); Wikipedia's page on the year says the Senate recognized him on 21 December. Vitellius had asked to be called Caesar a few days before (3:58). Titus is not in Book 3: Josephus says Vespasian sent him to Jerusalem (War 4.658).
r: Histories of Tacitus 2:79; Histories of Tacitus 3:58; Luke 2:1; Mark 12:17

t: A verb-less sentence in the Latin
p: The Latin as printed reads "Patrem illi Luceriam," with no verb. The translation follows the older English.
b: Fisher's Latin begins this section Patrem illi Luceriam: "illi" ("to him") and two accusatives (patrem, "father"; Luceriam, "Luceria") with no verb, so the sentence cannot be read as printed. Church and Brodribb's English reads it as "Luceria was his native place," and the Conversational English Translation keeps that sense. The Latin as printed has no word for "native place." The site gives no repair of the Latin. See the variant.
